{{Short description|English chemist}}
'''Dennis Frederick Evans''' {{postnominals|FRS}} (7 March 1928 – 6 November 1990) was an English chemist who made important contributions to nuclear magnetic resonance, magnetochemistry and other aspects of chemistry.
 
==Early life==
Evans was born in Nottingham, England on 28 March 1928. His father George Frederick Evans was a master carpenter and his mother (née Gladys Martha Taylor) was a dressmaker. He was educated at Huntingdon Street Junior School and then won a scholarship to Nottingham High School. In 1946 he entered Oxford with a scholarship to [[Lincoln College, Oxford|Lincoln College]] where his tutor was [[Rex Richards (chemist)|Rex Richards]] (later Sir Rex Richards FRS). He won the university Gibbs Prize in Chemistry in 1949, and in that year started DPhil work with Richards on [[calorimetry]] and the magnetic properties of clathrates containing nitric oxide or oxygen; nine papers resulted from this work. He was an ICI Research Fellow from 1952-5.<ref name="Green Griffith 2000 pp. 165–175" /> In 1953-4 he became a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Chicago with [[Robert S. Mulliken]] working on the electronic spectra of halogens in organic solvents, producing four papers under his own name.<ref name="Green Griffith 2000 pp. 165–175">{{cite journal | last1=Green | first1=M.L.H. | last2=Griffith | first2=W.P. | title=Dennis Frederick Evans. 27 March 1928 — 6 November 1990 | journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society | volume=46 | year=2000 | doi=10.1098/rsbm.1999.0078  | doi-access=free| pages=165–175| s2cid=73152090 }}</ref>

==Career and research==
In October 1955 [[Geoffrey Wilkinson]] appointed him as a lecturer in inorganic chemistry at [[Imperial College London]]. He was subsequently promoted to Senior Lecturer in 1963, Reader in 1964 and Professor in 1981. He was awarded an FRS in 1981.

His research interests ranged widely over a number of topics in inorganic, organic and physical chemistry. Here we select just three areas which made a lasting contribution to chemistry.

I. Measurement of [[magnetic susceptibility]]. For [[paramagnetic]]  inorganic materials in particular, such measurements are often useful. In 1959, he devised a procedure, now called the Evans Method, in which an NMR tube containing the paramagnetic species is dissolved in water-''tert''-butanol in the presence of a capillary of pure ''tert-''butanol. From the difference in positions of the <sup>1</sup>H NMR peak of the hydroxyl peak of pure butanol and the same peak shifted by the paramagnetic substrate the susceptibility of the sample can be calculated.<ref name="Evans 1959 p=2003">{{cite journal | last=Evans | first=D. F. | title=400. The determination of the paramagnetic susceptibility of substances in solution by nuclear magnetic resonance | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society | year=1959 | doi=10.1039/jr9590002003 | page=2003}}</ref><ref name="Evans Fazakerley Phillips 1971 p=1931">{{cite journal | last1=Evans | first1=D. F. | last2=Fazakerley | first2=G. V. | last3=Phillips | first3=R. F. | title=Organometallic compounds of bivalent europium, ytterbium, and samarium | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society A | year=1971 | doi=10.1039/j19710001931 | page=1931}}</ref> In 1967 he devised an ingenious modification of the classical [[Gouy balance]] in which,  instead of weighing the sample in a magnetic field,  a small but powerful magnet was weighed against the static sample.<ref name="Evans 1967 pp. 1670–1671">{{cite journal | last=Evans | first=D. F. | title=A simple Gouy–Rankine balance for measuring magnetic susceptibilities of solid paramagnetic substances | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society A | year=1967 | doi=10.1039/j19670001670 | pages=1670–1671}}</ref> This was further refined in 1974<ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.1088/0022-3735/7/4/007|title=A new type of magnetic balance|year=1974|last1=Evans|first1=D. F.|journal=Journal of Physics E |volume=7|issue=4|pages=247–249|bibcode=1974JPhE....7..247E}}</ref> by using two 6 g. strong magnets, each mounted on a torsion strip. The force that the static paramagnetic sample exerted on one magnet was balanced out by a current passed through a coil placed between the poles of the second magnet; by measurement of this current the magnetic susceptibility of the sample can be calculated.

II  [[Nuclear magnetic resonance]] spectroscopy (NMR). In addition to his use of NMR to determine magnetic susceptibilities of species in solution (see above) he made wide use of the technique in the study of organometallic and coordination complexes. He also used the technique of double irradiation of organic compounds to establish the relative signs of coupling constants.<ref name="Royal Society of Chemistry (RSC) 1961 p=185">{{cite journal | title=One Hundred and Twentieth Annual General Meeting | journal=Proceedings of the Chemical Society | issue= | year=1961 | doi=10.1039/ps9610000185 | page=185}}</ref><ref name="Evans 1962 pp. 183–187">{{cite journal | last=Evans | first=D.F. | title=The relative signs of fluorine N.M.R. spin coupling constants by double irradiation | journal=Molecular Physics | volume=5 | issue=2 | year=1962 | doi=10.1080/00268976200100181 | pages=183–187| bibcode=1962MolPh...5..183E }}</ref>

III Inorganic chemistry. He made a number of studies on [[Organometallic chemistry|organometallic]] and coordination complexes. An example of his ingenuity in this area is to show that divalent [[lanthanides]] might show [[Grignard reagent|Grignard]]-like behaviour, and to this end he found that samarium, europium and ytterbium formed such species<ref name="Evans Fazakerley Phillips 1970 p=244">{{cite journal | last1=Evans | first1=D. F. | last2=Fazakerley | first2=G. V. | last3=Phillips | first3=R. F. | title=Organometallic compounds of bivalent ytterbium | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society D | issue=4 | year=1970 | doi=10.1039/c29700000244 | page=244}}</ref><ref name="Evans Fazakerley Phillips 1971 p=1931">{{cite journal | last1=Evans | first1=D. F. | last2=Fazakerley | first2=G. V. | last3=Phillips | first3=R. F. | title=Organometallic compounds of bivalent europium, ytterbium, and samarium | journal=Journal of the Chemical Society A | year=1971 | doi=10.1039/j19710001931 | page=1931}}</ref> and that they showed Grignard-type reactions.<ref name="Evans Fazakerley Phillips 1971 p=1931" />

==Personal life==
Evans was looked upon fondly by people close to him, giving freely of his time and his immense knowledge (which was not confined to chemistry) to all who asked for help. Evans donated his time to assist those who asked for his assistance in a variety of topics, not nessesarly confined to chemistry. He kept a range of exotic pets, such as a Cayman Islands alligator and a five-foot sand snake called George fed with live toads obtained from his local Chelsea pub. George escaped into the King’s Road and was after re-capture given by Evans to the [[London Zoo]]. He also kept locusts (some of these escaped too), bird-eating lizards and giant scorpions. He became a celebrated member of the [[Chelsea Arts Club]].
